video_title: Lawfare Daily: A Progress Report on the War on Terrorism with Peter Bergen
gist: Peter Bergen reviews 25 years of the US war on terror (costs, missed chances at Tora Bora and with the Taliban, what worked institutionally) and argues that a light-footprint, long-duration presence is the least-bad model. The most market-relevant part is his view of the ongoing US-Iran war: with the Houthis effectively closing the Red Sea route to Suez, Brent recently at $108, a Fed hike and strains in private credit, he warns of a 'disharmonic convergence' damaging the US and global economy, and says the only way out is a negotiated hurting-stalemate deal that gives Iran some oil-sanctions relief and more control over Hormuz.

themes.theme: Iran war: energy chokepoints and macro contagion

insights.claim: Bergen says the Houthis entering the US-Iran conflict has effectively closed the straits leading to the Suez Canal, which he puts at about 13% of global shipping, while the Strait of Hormuz carries about 20% of global oil and gas.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Both major Middle East shipping chokepoints are under pressure at once, which supports elevated freight rates, tanker rates and energy risk premia.
insights.quote: So 13% of global shipping goes through the sewers canal and 20% of global oil and gas go through the straight of Hormuz. We have really snookered ourselves

insights.claim: Bergen notes that Brent crude was at $108 a barrel a few days before the recording and that the Fed had just raised interest rates for the first time in a while, against a background of the Saudis back at war with the Houthis and the US at war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: A war-driven oil shock arriving alongside Fed tightening is a stagflationary mix; watch oil-sensitive equities, rate expectations and duration risk.
insights.quote: I see that the Fed just raised interest rates for the first time in a while. Brent crude was at $108 a barrel just like a few days ago.

insights.claim: Bergen, who says he is no expert on markets, observes that private credit investors are trying to withdraw money but are hitting redemption caps, and warns that this, the oil shock and the war could combine into a convergence that damages the US and global economy.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Gated redemptions in private credit plus an energy shock is a channel for broader financial stress; watch BDC and private-credit fund flows and redemption-gate news.
insights.quote: look at the private credit market, people are trying to get their money out, but they're not really succeeding because they're kind of caps on what you can take out

insights.claim: Bergen argues that the Trump administration seems paralyzed with no real plan to end the Iran conflict, and says he no longer believes much of what the administration says about it because its statements have shifted.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Discount official de-escalation headlines; if there is no credible exit plan, the chokepoint disruption could last longer than markets price.
insights.quote: I don't believe very much what the administration says about this anymore because they've said a bunch of different things

insights.claim: Bergen frames the war as a mutually recognized hurting stalemate, so the only realistic way out is a least-bad negotiated deal. In it, Iran would likely get some oil-sanctions relief and somewhat more control over the Strait of Hormuz, perhaps dressed up as fees for environmental damage rather than tolls for passage.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: A settlement would likely add Iranian barrels back to supply (bearish for oil) but leave a lasting Iranian say over Hormuz transit, which would keep some structural risk premium.
insights.quote: Iranians would get some oil sanctions relief. You know, it would be painful, but we would have to, I think, allow them some greater control over the straight than they have now.

insights.claim: Bergen says any new deal with Iran will be worse than the 2015 nuclear deal, and calls Trump's 2018 withdrawal from a working deal the original sin and the current war an unforced error.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Expect settlement terms that favor Iran more than 2015 did, which matters for sanctions-relief timing and Iranian export volumes.
insights.quote: the original sin in this case was you Trump pulling out of a deal that was working in 2018

insights.claim: Bergen would advise taking the win, declaring Iran's program obliterated, rather than escalating. Citing an interview with former CENTCOM commander General Votel, he says seizing Kharg Island, about 12 miles off Iran's coast, would take a lot, and the US has so far avoided that mistake.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: A ground operation against Iran's main oil export terminal would be a major escalation and an oil spike trigger; its absence so far points to a ceiling on escalation.

insights.claim: Bergen argues that the Houthis act on their own strategic interests, which line up with Iran's even more than any orders from Tehran would, and that bombing them has a poor record: Saudi Arabia ran about 20,000 air strikes in the first anti-Houthi war before MBS ended it with little gained.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Air campaigns are unlikely to reopen Red Sea shipping quickly, so plan for prolonged Suez diversions rather than a fast military fix.

themes.theme: Costs and verdict on 25 years of war

insights.claim: Bergen tallies the war on terror's costs at about 200,000 Iraqi civilian deaths, 45,000 Afghan civilian deaths, 66,000 Afghan police and military deaths, about 7,000 US service members, and roughly 8,000 American contractors who got almost no media attention, plus $6 trillion in current and projected US taxpayer money.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: The scale of past spending shapes political appetite and fiscal room for new large deployments, including in the Iran war.

insights.claim: Bergen cites the US Army's official history of the Iraq war, the only official history since there was never an Iraq war commission, which concluded that Iran was the sole winner of the war.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Iran's regional reach today grew in part from the Iraq war, which helps explain its current leverage over the Gulf and Red Sea chokepoints.
insights.quote: that concluded that the sole winner of the Iraq war was Iran

insights.claim: Bergen argues that the Iraq war and the 2008 financial crisis together explain why Americans deeply distrust their elites. The Iraq war, he says, hobbled Hillary Clinton, enabled Obama and helped Trump, with terrorism top of mind during the ISIS peak.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Long-run distrust of elites caps public support for drawn-out foreign wars, which pushes toward deals over escalation.
insights.quote: there's a reason that Americans are very suspicious of their elites because they seem to have absolutely no idea what they're doing

insights.claim: Bergen says the Iraq war resuscitated a badly damaged al-Qaeda, as the National Intelligence Estimate concluded, and produced al-Qaeda in Iraq, which later became ISIS.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Large interventions can create the threats they aim to remove, which argues for skepticism toward escalation narratives in the current conflict.
insights.quote: the estimate said essentially the Iraq War resuscitated this group, which is true

insights.claim: Bergen calls letting bin Laden escape at Tora Bora a major error: Jim Mattis's request to deploy his 1,500 Marines was never answered, and General Tommy Franks turned down CIA commander Gary Berntsen's request for a battalion of Rangers on what Bergen calls specious reasoning.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Historical context for how command decisions can waste a decisive moment; no direct trade.

insights.claim: Bergen argues that the real missed peace opportunity with the Taliban was their December 5, 2001 surrender to Karzai, not the Bonn conference. Rumsfeld vetoed Karzai's offer of amnesty, and each later delay worsened the US position until the Trump-era talks in 2018 produced a terrible bargain.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Negotiating terms get worse the longer a party waits past its point of maximum strength, which applies to the current Iran stalemate as well.

insights.claim: Bergen says that by treating the Taliban and al-Qaeda as the same group, the US muddled its goals and created a self-fulfilling prophecy, as the Taliban adopted IEDs and suicide attacks.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Misclassifying adversaries can harden them, which bears on the current terrorist designations of cartels.

insights.claim: Bergen says expecting Pakistan to act against its own national security interest was childish. He relays that General Kayani told Ambassador Ryan Crocker that Pakistan was hedging its bets on the Taliban because it expected the US to leave, as it had after the Soviet withdrawal.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Regional actors hedge against US staying power; expect Gulf states and others to do the same in the Iran conflict.
insights.quote: we know you left in the 1980s after the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan

insights.claim: Bergen argues that designating drug cartels as foreign terrorist organizations wastes effort and devalues the label, since the DEA and US Customs already cover them and, by definition, a criminal group is not a terrorist organization.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Terrorist designations of cartels widen sanctions and material-support exposure; firms with Latin American supply chains or banking ties should watch compliance risk.
insights.quote: By definition, a criminal group is not a terrorist organization.

themes.theme: Go light, go long: what worked

insights.claim: Bergen's main lesson is that, after avoiding war if possible, the least-bad approach is 'go light, go long': a small, persistent US presence acting as a force multiplier. He points to the campaign against ISIS led by Iraq's Golden Division and the largely Kurdish SDF, which was politically and financially sustainable with few American deaths.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: A light-footprint model means continued spending on ISR, drones and special operations rather than mass troop deployments.
insights.quote: persistent level of relatively small numbers of American troops can really be a false multiplier

insights.claim: Bergen says the anti-ISIS campaign came at a heavy cost, about 35,000 American air strikes with Mosul nearly turned into a parking lot, and suggests the next step is far more precise armed drones to reduce how much air power is used.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Supports demand for precision munitions and armed-drone programs over large-scale air campaigns.

insights.claim: Bergen argues that counterinsurgency is a set of tactics rather than a strategy, mostly common sense, and could not solve Iraq's underlying Sunni-Shia civil war. He says what really mattered was the Awakening, which put 100,000 Sunni tribal fighters on the US payroll against al-Qaeda in Iraq.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Tactical military success does not resolve political fault lines, so be skeptical of claims that military operations alone end a conflict.
insights.quote: counterinsurgency is as a set of tactics. It's not really anything strategic and most of it is common sense

insights.claim: Bergen cites the NSA's recently declassified Real Time Regional Gateway, which in 2005 understood the content of about a million phone calls a day in Iraq and tracked who was calling whom across about 100 million calls a day. He also names JSOC, special forces, advise-and-assist, TSA, the NCTC and the growth of Joint Terrorism Task Forces from 30 to more than 100 as reforms that worked.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: These are lasting institutional and budget lines (signals intelligence, special operations, homeland security) that are likely to persist across administrations.
insights.quote: we understood the content of a million phone calls a day in Baghdad in Iraq in 2005

themes.theme: Jihadist missteps and al-Sharaa's pragmatic Syria

insights.claim: Bergen says bin Laden misread US resolve from the Beirut 1983 and Somalia 1993 withdrawals. He and his co-founder Abu Hafs expected any US response to 9/11 to look like the casualty-free 1999 Kosovo air war, and Bergen calls Zawahiri a minor player rather than al-Qaeda's brains.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Adversaries tend to extrapolate past US restraint; a misread of resolve is a recurring escalation risk.

insights.claim: Bergen describes Syrian President al-Sharaa's path from leading al-Qaeda in Syria, through running services in Idlib from 2015, to running the whole country. He took advantage of Iran and Russia being weakened, including by the 2025 Israel-US war on Iran, and now seems more interested in foreign direct investment than jihad.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Syria is opening to foreign investment under a pragmatic leader, an early-stage frontier-market and reconstruction story with high governance risk.
insights.quote: he seems much more interested in foreign direct investment than you know supporting you know some g you know uh cause around the world

insights.claim: The host notes that credit cards are now usable in Syria for the first time in a long time, a sign that Syria is beginning to join the somewhat functional Middle Eastern states.
insights.speaker: Host (Daniel Byman)
insights.so_what: Reconnection to payment networks is a concrete marker of Syria's financial normalization and easing sanctions; watch card networks and regional banks entering.

insights.claim: Bergen predicts that an armed drone attack of significant size on the United States, by an empowered individual or a non-state actor, is highly predictable soon. He notes that private military contractors, including the former Blackwater, have killed more than a thousand people with armed drones fighting Haitian gangs.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Supports a tailwind for counter-drone systems, airspace security and drone-detection vendors.
insights.quote: we're going to have an armed drone attack on the United States of some level of problematic size

insights.claim: Bergen takes AI leaders' warnings about AI-enabled synthetic biology at face value, since they come from scientists rather than politicians as in the 2003 WMD hype. He notes that in August Stanford scientists created 18 new de novo viruses, benign ones, and asks whether an attacker like Bruce Ivins could do far worse with AI.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Biosecurity, biosurveillance and AI-safety regulation are likely to become policy priorities, with possible regulatory spillover onto AI and synthetic-biology firms.

insights.claim: Bergen judges the likelihood of al-Qaeda attacking the United States in any meaningful way to be pretty low, though he notes that ISIS-K killed 140 people in Moscow just over a year ago, so these groups still have reach.
insights.speaker: Peter Bergen
insights.so_what: Mass-casualty jihadist attacks on the US homeland are a lower tail risk than drone or bio threats.
insights.quote: I think the likelihood of al-Qaeda attacking the United States in any meaningful way is pretty low
